###### Executive Summary 

Copper Quarterly July 2009   Executive Summary 

## Executive Summary Outlook totally reliant on China 



- At current prices mines are not cutting back.  Indeed some re-openings have been announced.  The onus has shifted to smelters and refineries, with the issue of excess supply and poor copper demand eclipsing those of concentrate availability. 



- Copper demand is expected to fall sharply this year outside of China and fabricators are preparing extended summer shut downs.  However, Chinese growth is forecast to be higher than previously expected due to higher scrap replacement and restocking effects. 



- Scrap availability fell sharply in Q4 2008 and Q1 2009, as weak economic activity cut scrap generation and low prices trimmed the flow of material to the market.  Higher prices in Q2 led to an improvement in availability, reducing cathode replacement for scrap at semi fabricators. 



- Strategic government purchases (Chinese SRB and Korean PPS) have now abated, although they are likely to resume if prices ease back.  In addition, Chinese cathode imports in H1 of 1.8Mt are expected to be followed by a decline, as the arbitrage window has closed. 



- Demand growth in China is expected to ease in H2 and remain poor elsewhere, so the market should move into surplus.  With most of this accumulating in the world outside of China and assumed to end up in exchange warehouses, LME prices are likely to come under pressure. 



- However, restocking driven growth in H1 2010 should see the market move into deficit and prices rise back towards $5,000/t.  In H2 2010, prices will come off as production grows but demand slows as restocking growth ends, leading to rising surpluses and falling prices. 



- In 2011 prices will start the year at a low ebb and a stock overhang will keep them from rising rapidly, despite a modest annual deficit.  Thereafter, though, above average demand growth will be met by modest supply growth, leading to higher deficits and rising prices.

###### Ahead of the game 

Despite a significant underlying market surplus, copper prices have been distorted so far this year.  Chinese buying due to State Reserves Bureau (SRB) and consumer restocking, and scrap replacement have all played a role in boosting prices, alongside a weaker US dollar and Korean Public Procurement Service (PPS) purchases.  World refined copper consumption in 2009 is expected to be down by around 10.1% year-on-year.  Excluding China, where consumption is set to expand by 10.3%, the decline is closer to 17.9%. 

The market has focussed on the level of exchange stocks (declining) and Chinese imports (rising) which has led to the perceived tightness in the market and supported prices at much higher levels than anyone expected.  Economic realities have taken a back seat. 

At current price levels, we are unlikely to see any further cutbacks at the mines; $3,500/t (real prices) is a critical level.  Indeed some re-openings have been announced.  Concentrates remain in tight supply but the issue of availability is being eclipsed by that of the excess supply of sulphuric acid and weaker demand for refined copper.  Smelters and refineries have as a result announced some cutbacks.  Yet the global market for refined metal is still in a surplus. Over the first half of this year the market outside of China was broadly in balance as China gorged on any available copper.  Outside of China the significant Q1 surplus was matched by an equally large Q2 deficit, which helps to explain the run up in prices over the last quarter. 

###### **Chinese market oversupplied** 

The tidal wave of Chinese imports, however, has not been fully absorbed into demand downstream.  Before the distorting effect of SRB purchasing, the Chinese copper market was in a 600,000t surplus in H1.  Around 235,000t can be accounted for by SRB restocking, leaving the market with an excess of almost 400,000t.  The SRB has stated that for now its purchasing

We anticipate that given that the arbitrage window of opportunity has all but disappeared and that it is unlikely we will see buying of this order repeated over the second half of the year, prices should come under some downward pressure. The extent of the fall is likely to be lower than previous expectations, even though demand outside of China has yet to begin to recover. We expect 2010 to be a tale of two halves. Restocking led growth in the world outside of China will be concentrated in H1, pushing the global market into deficit and driving prices up to an average of $4,700/t in Q2. The market balance will move into a significant surplus in H2 against a backdrop of sequential refined production growth and anaemic underlying demand and receding restocking. Moreover, the modest draw down in stocks through H1 means that, based on the fundamentals, a fall in prices is required if the imbalance is to be kept under control. We therefore expect prices to average $3,500/t in Q4 2010. We have not significantly altered our outlook for 2011-2013 from that presented in April. Consumption growth will outpace that of production and the market will move back into deficit by 2011. However, prices will be at a low level at the beginning of the year and the inventory built up over 2009 and 2010 will restrain the price increase such that the annual average will be $1.66/lb ($3,650/t) that year. 2011 will be the low point in the price cycle and will result in mine cutbacks and put a brake on project developments. Prices will begin to rise again as stocks are drawn down in 2012 and 2013. ###### Consumption – brought forward Since the last quarterly our fundamental outlook has not changed. Demand is weak outside of China, India and the GCC (Gulf Cooperation Council) region and there have been no further announcement of cutbacks at either the mines or the smelters due to prices or demand. CRU International Limited confidential 4 Copper Quart

erly July 2009 Executive Summary The key change since the last Quarterly is sentiment. Over the past three months, alongside the positive tone from the financial sector, copper has rallied to highs of $5,381/t on the back of what now appears to have been an over-hyped expectation that a fully fledged global economic recovery was underway. Simply, this has been a restocking cycle initially fed by the run up in copper prices. There is accumulating evidence that the escalation in Chinese imports of refined cathode to replace scrap and fuel the investment driven Chinese rebound has now come to an end. The sequential quarter-on-quarter rally in consumption, particularly in Korea, Taiwan and China over the first half of this year has also abated as demand is tempered at the higher prices. We anticipate that demand overall in the current quarter will remain subdued as the majority of semis plants maintain a short working week and the usual summer breaks are extended. Taiwan China
There are some improving indicators for copper from the GCC states and India, which are performing better than anticipated, all of which are being domestically driven. This is particularly supportive given that the developed economies are suffering a significant contraction in demand. Japan is expected to contract by more than a third and W Europe and N. America by nearly 20% year-on-year in 2009. Russia is also set to experience a 50% slump in demand as the removal of export tariffs for copper cathode has resulted in a switch in exports to copper cathode from copper wirerod, a factor not widely known and appreciated. ###### **Wire & Cable is the key to recovery** From an end use perspective, there is no sign of a recovery from the wire and cable sector, whilst the situation at brass mills is even worse. What we have seen to-date is a seasonal rise and an element of restocking. If there is no pull through from the end-use sector then there is the clear potential for a shallow secondary dip in demand this summer and the possibility of a second wave of weakness in 2010. China remains the key support to demand with consumption set to expand by 10.3%. Consumption growth has been supported by the Government’s 4 trillion yuan (US$586B) stimulus package, tight scrap availability and SRB strategic stockpiling. Demand is expected to soften in the second half of this year as the impact of the stimulus package, particularly in the power sector, begins to wane. South Korean demand has also held up particularly well, boosted by robust wirerod production. However, much of this demand has been front loaded (brought forward) over the first half of the year boosted by power cable orders from the state power utility, which has been encouraged to spend almost two thirds of its annual budget in H1. A weak H2 could unfold. Certainly all the signs are in place for poor performance in H2 with extended summer holidays, the impact of frontloading of demand in Korea (boosted by power cable orders) and China. This would remove the support that has propelled prices higher thus far. The higher copper prices in H1 have also improved the scrap pipeline potential for the second half, possibly weakening another support pin for cathode demand. There is also the concern that consumers may run out of fixed procurement budgets if the price of copper remains at these higher levels. In Nov/De

c 2008 demand for cathode nosedived.  As a consequence it is likely that we will see a year-on-year increase in Nov/Dec this year, but these are usually low volume months and are likely to remain so again this year. 

Substitution issues have not gone away.  The development of aluminium automotive harnessing wire is moving forward driven by both a cost reduction as well as a light-weighting incentive.  Aluminium clad copper (ACC) is also threatening to capture market share in air

###### **Substitution or rationing?** 

We expect refined consumption (ex-China) to begin to recover in 2010, with a global increase of 6.8%, slowing to 2.2% by 2013.  By 2011 production will no longer be high enough to meet demand and the refined market will shift to deficit, although a stock overhang will weigh on prices.  Prices will respond later as inventories are drawn down while the deficit remains in place to 2013.  Fundamental longer-term tightness threatens to accelerate substitution pressures in the medium-term, or else demand in non-critical, low value added applications will be rationed regionally and globally. 

###### Production – pressure shifts from mines to smelters and refineries 

The drop in price in Q4 2008, while brutal, was brief.  As we noted in our previous quarterly producers’ immediate reaction was a series of mine cutbacks, particularly by the marginal players, some of which are now slowly coming back on stream given the higher than anticipated copper prices.  Copper producers were also swift to review their project pipelines and, with the era of easy money now over and a more stringent financing climate, project development will remain constrained.  Moreover, given the strong recovery in prices, it is now unlikely that producers will be as swift to react to price declines by curtailing operating output.  Rather they are likely to focus on delaying project developments, especially given that the anticipated closures outlined in our April Quarterly have not been forthcoming. 

At current prices there is no incentive for producers to cut back, and based on preliminary indications mine output should hold up in Q2 and the remainder of 2009.  The strain has now shifted to the smelters and refineries, given the oversupply in the sulphuric acid market (smelters produce acid as a by-product) and the poor outlook for refined demand.  Moreover, further curtailments at the refined level could occur at Japanese and South Korean smelters, if the Chinese follow through with action on their anti-dumping investigation into sul

phuric acid imports from those countries. The absence of the anticipated cutbacks at the mines has eased the tightness in the concentrates market, with a smaller than previously forecast deficit set to remain in place over the second half of the year. The pressure to cut back has now been transferred to the smelters and refineries and for 2009 we are now forecasting a decline in smelter and electrorefined output as cutbacks are expected to more than offset any increases in capacity. Utilisation rates will fall from an average of 72% in 2008 down to just 66% in 2009. The two factors, excess supply of sulphuric acid and poor copper demand, are expected to be the main forces behind the forecast level of smelter cutbacks for the next two years. It will be those smelters most vulnerable to the spot acid market that would likely have to curtail production if they are unable to offload their by-product acid. Tight scrap availability will also limit the level of secondary output. The shortfall in concentrate availability will still be a factor, but will be less significant. Although there have been no major cutback/closure announcements for 2009 since our last report, we understand that Brazilian producer Caraiba reduced its refined copper output during CRU International Limited confidential Copper Quarterly July 2009 Executive Summary 7 the first quarter due to rising stocks of sulphuric acid. Further ahead, HudBay has announced that it will be closing its Flin Flon smelter and White Pine refinery in 2010. The smelter was due to close before 2013 for environmental reasons and given the current concentrates and sulphuric acid markets the company has decided to bring this forward to 2010. ###### **Mixed picture on restocking** 

It is necessary for us to consider the implications of several different sorts of inventory effects in our analysis.  Indications are that there has been little build-up of cathode inventory by fabricators, who have also avoided building up their own semis inventory.  High prices and some rundown in stocks in Q4 mean that their inventory levels are minimal.  However, we believe that certain traders and speculators are now holding substantial stocks, particularly in China, and this explains why our refined consumption figures for China are much lower than import and domestic production levels may suggest.  We only count cathode as being consumed when it is melted in furnaces. 

Stocks of semis held by end-users are still reported to be low in most regions.  Wire and cable inventory levels are also generally quite low. In many areas of the cable industry, such as utility power cable, cable is made to order and so stocks are not really an issue. For products such as automotive wire and appliance wire and some winding wire, just in time manufacturing practices are used so stock levels are normally low.  All this suggests that when economic conditions recover, copper demand is likely to recover with them.  However, a slow recovery in demand will also mean a slow recovery in inventories. 

###### **Substitution remains an issue, but outweighed by economic factors** 

Substitution from copper to other materials has not disappeared during the current crisis, but has perhaps lessened in significance and visibility, due to the much larger impact on refined demand of the economic slowdown.  Nevertheless, it remains a factor.  Whilst the absolute price of copper has fallen (although it remains historically high), the ratio between the copper price and the price of the most frequent substitute aluminium has not – in fact, this remains over the 3:1 ratio that CRU has previously identified as a major driver of substitution. 

In volume terms, copper faces the biggest ongoing threat in the utility power cable sector. Alcoa recently reported that it has been very successful in supplying aluminium to this sector rather than copper, particularly in China.  In this market, most utility po

wer cables use aluminium rather than copper. Elsewhere, the ongoing shifts away from copper are continuing in the plumbing and telecoms sectors and these are long-term, irreversible trends. Automotive wiring harnesses are also seeing continued substitution away from copper (see Japan section). Some continued substitution is also ongoing in the winding and utility wire segments. In the case of air conditioner tube, cutbacks in expenditure mean that research and development budgets have been slashed, which has slowed development work towards using aluminium rather than copper. The American Bureau of Metal Statistics (ABMS) reported in July that US apparent refined copper consumption totalled 117,027t in May, 26.8% lower than May 2008. Year-to-date consumption declined 29.9% from the same period last year. Domestic shipments fell by 14.5% y-o-y but it was noted that US LME warehouse inventories were falling, with some 500t and 5,528t being exported from New Orleans to China and Italy respectively. Demand in the US construction market remained weak in Q2 2009 although it showed signs of improvement towards the end of the quarter. Total construction spending slipped 0.9% y-o-y to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of US$964B in May, the lowest rate of decline in 5 years. Residential construction spending declined 33.3% y-o-y and 3.5% m-o-m to a seasonally adjusted rate of US$247B while non-residential construction spending dropped 0.4% y-o-y but increased 0.1% m-o-m (since April was particularly weak) to a seasonally adjusted rate of US$717B. CRU International Limited confidential 20 Copper Quarterly Report July 2009 Chapter 1 Market participants have mixed opinion about the outlook of the US construction industry. Some believe that the market is bottoming out as people are generally more optimistic about the economy but others argue that a recovery, particularly in construction, is not within sight yet. CRU believes that the latter argument is more convincing, with the latest evidence coming from non-residential construction. Demand for commercial buildings did not see any improvement in the first two quarters and apparently the problem is spreading across the US. Q2 office vacancy rates of Washington D.C., Northern Virginia and suburban Maryland increased to 10.2%, 13.9% and 13.9% respectively, according to a report by CB Richard Ellis. There is also a growing trend of subleasing in non-residential real estate. Given the dire situation in credit availability, more project delays and cancellations are expected. The construction industry now has the highest unemployment rate of 17.4% in the US, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. ###### **3.1.2 Brass mill products** 

CRU believes that there was no dramatic change in the US brass mill industry as both semis consumption and production remained low during Q2.  Fabricators are trying their best to retain their profits (or to reduce losses) through strict cost discipline and restructuring programmes. 

Our current data suggests that copper tube consumption declined by more than 30% y-o-y in the US while domestic production followed the trend closely and fell by almost the same percentage during the first quarter of the year.  Trade data from the Global Trade Atlas indicates there was a slight improvement in copper tube imports during March but fell again in April.  In May, import volume was up 13% from April to 8,534t while exports totalled 1,739t compared to 2,174t in April.  Import volume for the first five months in 2009 totalled 39,077t, 27% down on the same period last year.  Lower US copper tube export volume to Mexico was the main reason for the decline.  This is possibly due to the new commercial tube capacity, which is estimated to be around 110,000t being commissioned by the end of the year, at **Luvata** and **Henan Golden Dragon** in Mexico.  These plants are likely to put competitive pressure on the US producers not only in Mexico but also in the US. **Wolverine Tube** reported that it managed to cut its net loss to US$48.5M for the fiscal

year ended 31<sup>st</sup> December 2008, compared to a loss of US$98.2M a year ago.  Net sales in 2008 were US$816M, 19% below a year ago and the decline was attributed to the discontinuance of plumbing tube manufacturing at its Decatur facility in December 2007.  Previously, the company‘s weak profitability has forced it to raise cash from an exchange offer for its Senior Notes in April 2009. 

In July, **Mueller Industries Inc** , a leading copper tube and fittings manufacturer, announced its second quarter results. US factory shipments of air conditioners and air-source heat pumps for April amounted to 410,932 units, 23% below April 2008, said the **Air-Conditioning Heating and Refrigeration Institute** .  Year-to-date combined shipments totalled 1,366,249 units, down by 24% compared to the same period a year ago. 

The **Semiconductor Industry Association** reported that the 3-month moving average dollar amounts of world semiconductor shipments totalled US$16.5B in May 2009, down 23.2% y-o-y but up 5.4% from April 2009.  3-month moving average of shipments to America fell by 19.4% y-o-y to US$2.7B.  The association said that the third-consecutive month of sequential growth for the semiconductor industry led it to be cautiously optimistic about a return to normal seasonal patterns for the industry going forward. 

###### 3.3 Canada & Mexico 

It is reported there has been stability in Canadian wirerod demand but not a noticeable uptick in Q2.  We believe that fabricators are currently operating on average for 3-4 days per week and will extend their summer shutdown by a week to keep inventory down.  CRU believes other companies in the wire and cable industry will operate at similar rate during July and August. The Canadian market is 8-12 months behind on the recession curve than the US.  Also, there was no housing bubble in Canada so house prices have only fallen by approximately 5% so far. Production fell rapidly in November last year and hit a low with production down by around 25% y-o-y.  CRU estimates that total Canadian refined consumption fell by 35% y-o-y to 32,000t in Q2 and will drop 20% y-o-y to 35,000t in Q3.   We predict that refined copper consumption will amount to 134,000t for the whole year, down from 161,000t in 2008. 

Mexican copper consumption is estimated to decline by 26% this year, followed by a 12.3% bounce back in 2010.  This double-digit increase is mainly due to the new copper tube capacity at Mexico, which is starting to come online during the second half of 2009.  Despite the current economic conditions, a number of fabricators decided to go ahead with their expansion pl

ans. Luvata expects to begin production at its Monterrey, Mexico tube plant in Q3 2009.  The plant anticipates ramping up to full production of 50,000t by mid-2010.  However, CRU would not be surprised if weak market demand could delay progress of the plant.  Henan Golden Dragon plans to start production at its 60,000t Mexico plant in mid-2009.  Reports say that the plant is not affected by swine flu and is running at a satisfactory level.  IUSA also had plans to increase its production capacity.

###### 4.  Europe 

###### 4.1 Western European consumption stabilises 

CRU expects that Western Europe will see refined copper consumption plummet 19.7% y-o-y to 2.7Mt in 2009, with the first half of the year showing consumption dropping 27% compared to the same period last year.  We predict that demand will fall by 16% y-o-y in Q3.  Copper semis fabricators have mixed opinions about the outlook of copper demand for the second half of the year.  Most of them agree that there will not be an easy or speedy pick up within sight, assuming it is true that they have seen the bottom of the recession.  This is partly attributed to a seasonal effect that most of the mills will take a longer summer holiday this year which will affect semis production volumes.  Semis plants that have implemented short time working will also create an impact as this will limit their responsiveness even if demand bounces back earlier than expected.  One piece of good news is that demand from the end-use markets appear to have stabilised, albeit at a very low level. 

In the automotive sector, Western European motor vehicle production is predicted to decline by more than 30% in Q3.  French production will lead the fall by dropping 41.2% y-o-y while Italian production will fall by 40.9% y-o-y.  Germany and the UK will see relatively modest declines.  Indeed, latest reports suggest that the German automotive sector is seeing significant improvements from the previous quarter, not only because of the scrappage scheme, but also new orders due to foreign demand for German cars.  The Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders reported that new car registrations in the UK declined by 15.7% y-o-y in June to 176,264 units.  This was the smallest decline since July 2008, as the scrappage scheme has begun to have a positive impact on sales in the industry. 

**Nissan** saw sales increase in major European markets including Germany, France and Italy, which operate a scrappage scheme.  The UK scrappage scheme started in May.  The British government is offering a £1,000 incentive to be matched by participating manufacturers when scrapping a taxed, insured and MOT’d car more than ten years old which has been owned for at least one year.  The company said the Sunderland plant will employ 150 manufacturing staff to meet this temporary increase in demand.  However, the full-year forecasts still show a dep

ressed market. Taking into consideration the incentive created by the schemes, European automotive production will possibly see improvements in Q4, which would then feed into copper consumption by Q1 2010 at the earliest. Manufacturing production continues to fall at an unprecedented rate, according to a report by Markit. However, there are signs that the prolonged contraction may be easing. The Markit Eurozone Composite Output Index was 44.6 in June, compared to 44.0 in May. The decline in output was the smallest since September last year and is now being led by the service sector rather than the manufacturing sector. As for construction, CRU anticipates that France and Germany are seeing a slower rate of decline, which suggests that the market has seen the bottom. In Q3, construction in France is expected to decline by 4.3% y-o-y, compared to 5.8% decline in the previous quarter. The UK is still expecting a double-digit decline but the rate will be slower as soon as the government’s home buying subsidy scheme delivers its effect. However, demand from Spanish and Italian construction markets will remain grim for the rest of the year. Eurostat reported in July that the CRU International Limited confidential Copper Quarterly Report July 2009 Chapter 1 29 slump in Spanish construction has led to the highest rate of unemployment in the European Union at 18.7%. The construction sector has so far the worst outlook among the largest copper end-use markets, which in turns limits our hopes for a quick recovery in refined copper demand as products such as wirerod and tube are directly linked to building activity. One of the reasons why Italian wirerod demand is weaker is that in Southern European, the main market is enamelled wire and appliance wire and these products have been particularly badly hit compared to other wire and cable products.  In Spain, wirerod producers such as **Cunext** are supported by export opportunities to North Africa but local demand is as sluggish as everywhere else in Europe. ###### **4.1.2 Brass mill products** 

The market for copper semis products has been quiet throughout Q2 but it is apparent that mills are still having a hard time as copper semis production on average dropped by 30% y-o-y for the first half of the year with brass rod being the hardest hit.  As a result, CRU estimates that Western European refined copper consumption has fallen by 19.7% y-o-y in 2009, with Q2 demand dropping by 27% y-o-y to 707,000t. 

A court case that concerned several copper tube fabricators has caught our attention.  On 6<sup>th</sup> May, the European Union’s Court of Justice issued a press release regarding a fine of 78.7M euros (US$97M at December 2003 rates) imposed on the Finnish undertaking **Outokumpu** , the **KME Group** and the German company **Wieland-Werke** for taking part in a copper tube cartel during 1998 to 2001.  The Court of First Instance upheld the European Commission’s decision to impose the fine on the three companies.  The Court ruled that the Commission correctly increased the fine of KME and Wieland-Werke and did not make any obvious error in assessing the cooperation of these two companies.  In July, KME said that its subsidiaries (KME Germany, KME France and KME Italy) have appealed the court decision regarding their proportion of the fine. It also said in an earlier statement that the fine amount of 39.8M euros (US$49M at December 2003 rates) was wholly provisioned in the profit and loss accounts of FY2003. 

KME announced in May that its output volume in Q1 2009 dropped by 28% y-o-y to 113,700t

. The company said that the steep fall in production was due to the current gloomy economic conditions.  The hardest hit product segment was brass rod used in plumbing fixtures. Consolidated sales revenues in Q1 2009 are reported to have fallen by 45% y-o-y to 459M euros (US$626M).  Taking the value of raw materials into account, revenues totalled 174M euros (US$243M), 25% lower than the same period a year ago.  KME seems to be keen to restructure its organisation.  The company merged its Denmark operations with **Alumenco** to form a new company, **MetalCenter** , which will market copper and aluminium semi fabricated products. MetalCenter expects that sales in 2009 will exceed 20M euros (US$28M).  KME has also acquired 30% of **Metalbuyer S.p.A.** with an option to raise the stake to 51% and 30% of **Sigmet** , a company that specialises in ferrous and non-ferrous metals trading.  More acquisitions are expected this year as KME aims to create a network of European companies which conduct the same recycling business.

Market sentiment has been so good that a number of producers were confident to go ahead with new capacity plans. **Tiandilong Group** (Heaven and Earth Dragon) plans to go into production in May with its 250,000t 8mm copper wirerod production line. However, it depends how well the fabricators adjust their volumes to the market conditions.  A slowdown would also reduce the need for wirerod imports from South Korea, Taiwan and elsewhere. 

###### **Tube demand from air conditioner manufacturers improves** 

**Jiangsu Longda** , a tube manufacturer said that the current market for copper tube in China is weaker than it expected.  Given the slump in export markets, it estimates that domestic and international sales of the copper tube industry in the first six months of 2009 would be on average 25% lower than the same period in 2008.  The Chinese customs reported that exports of copper tube in the first five months of the year contracted by 24% y-o-y to 62,771t.  According to the National Bureau of Statistics of China, domestic room air conditioners production for the first half of the year was 20% down y-o-y.  However, **Jiangxi Copper** argues that demand for commercial tube is set to improve during the second half of the year.  The company has started to receive orders from air conditioner producers in July, which is a sign of restocking in the downstream market.  It said that the air conditioner producers have not prepared enough stocks or a price rebound and they will need to restock copper tubes.  Market participants also said that the major three air conditioner producers are seeing significant improvement in sales, given the hot weather this summer.  On top of that, government stimulus packages which target the home appliances market will give a boost to air conditioner consumption. 

Demand for copper alloy tube has remained stable as oil pipe and desalination pipe demand is supported by the government stimulus plan.  Copper alloy tube offtake from the Middle East also benefits local manufacturers.  China Metals reported that the utilisation rate at tube

###### **Market is still weak for brass rod and wire** 

The Chinese brass rod and wire industry has been less optimistic, compared to copper wirerod and copper tube fabricators.  Most of the producers we have spoken to said they are uncertain of the market outlook.  One major brass rod fabricator said the demand is really bad at the moment and it is not only because of the seasonal effect.  The plant is still running at full capacity but there are definitely no plans to expand in the near future.  This shows a big contrast from wirerod and tube producers, who have been keen to invest in new projects. 

###### **Copper flat rolled products demand picking up** 

The biggest end-use market of copper flat rolled products is the electrical and electronic product market.  Despite the global economic downturn, demand for these products has remained resilient in China.  In addition, a lot of offshoring activities into China over the past few years have secured its production share in the global market.  The recent 2B yuan (US$293M) subsidy for new purchases of home appliances will probably benefit the local flat rolled producers as this will trigger a quicker restocking process at their customers.  In fact, some major household appliances production already saw growth in May.  H1 numbers (excluding air conditioners) saw on average 4% growth y-o-y.  However, integrated circuit output for the first five months was still 21% down y-o-y. 

**Jingcheng Copper Co Ltd** , a copper and alloy sheet and strip fabricator in Anhui Province, announced that it will expand its high precision copper alloy sheet and strip project from 20,000t/y to 30,000t/y.  The plant will mainly produce brass strip for linker, socket connector, decorating, electronic equipment and other applications.  It is reported that the total investment of the project amounts to 495M yuan (US$73M) and it will take approximately two years to construct.  Jingcheng Copper has an annual capacity of 70,000t of copper and alloy sheet and strip.  The company generates production value of 2B yuan (US$293M). 

###### 5.2 Japan 

Japan continues to be the worst affected by the crisis in terms of refined copper demand, which we forecast will plummet this year, falling 36.9% y-o-y.  Volumes have recovered slightly month-on-month in the last few months, but we do not expect any major recovery this year. The worst performance is from the winding, appliance, and automotive wire sectors, where demand is down by between 40% and 50% as a result of a collapse in exports of electrical goods and equipment and the very hard time being faced by the automotive industry.

###### 5.3 South Korea 

South Korea has seen refined consumption hold up surprisingly well in 2009.  Our current forecast is that demand will fall by a modest 2.4% y-o-y, a significant improvement on our previous forecast.  Semis production has increased so far this year as a result of increased output of copper wirerod driven by strong power and ship cable demand, although other copper semis still show a y-o-y decline in volumes.  On the domestic front, however, the construction sector remains weak and the automotive sector has been hit hard by falling vehicle output.  South Korean vehicle production was down by 25.9% y-o-y to 269,000 units in April 2009, its 10<sup>th</sup> consecutive month of y-o-y decline.  Industrial production is expected to be down 7.8% this year.

###### 5.5 India 

We now anticipate positive growth in Indian refined copper consumption this year, up 7.3% y- o-y.  Production of copper wirerod in India was adversely affected last year by smelter shutdowns, but capacity is again ramping up.  Leading Indian wirerod fabricators saw a solid first quarter, with **Birla Copper** seeing output rise 15.1% y-o-y in Q1 2009 to 41,347t, although output at **Vedanta** was down 9.7% y-o-y in Q1 2009 to 56,000t (against a strong Q1 2008).  We expect wirerod production to remain steady.  The larger wirerod fabricators are benefitting from replacement of lower quality scrap based wirerod, both as cable manufacturers increasingly seek to use better quality wirerod, and also due to problems with scrap supply and financing. Vedanta has held discussions with Southwire about the possibility of adding a further wirerod line, but since the financial crisis, these have been put on hold for the time being. 

India’s semis-manufacturers are benefitting from the fact that demand is largely driven by the domestic market rather than being reliant on exports.  The expansion of India’s power infrastructure is continuing.  India has a persistent power deficit, and it remains highly important for the country to develop its power sector if it is to see continued economic growth. The power sector is budgeted to spend around US$230B between 2007-2012.  Investments in alternative energy are also substantial, particularly wind power, which uses more copper than conventional generation systems.  Other infrastructure development with a significant benefit for copper includes the planned electrification of 3,500km of rail per year between 2007-2012. 

Although the real estate sector has slowed due to the economic crisis, this will be a much shallower and shorter slump than in the developed world, with a recovery expected in the second half of this year. Indian industrial production is also forecast to continue to grow with a modest rise of 0.3% this year followed by growth of 6.4% in 2010.

The company produced 2,100t of wirerod in Q1, as opposed to 15,600t in the previous quarter and 13,400t in Q1 2008.

###### **6.1.1 Brazil** 

We expect Brazil to see refined copper demand contract by around 11.3% in 2009.  In response to the crisis, the government has cut Industrialized Products Tax (IPI) for many copper consuming products, including vehicles and white goods; this cut has recently been extended to building materials.  The measures are also credited with giving support to Brazilian car sales. Vehicle production in Brazil fell by 17.9% y-o-y to 1.1Mt in the first four months of 2009, but sales remained broadly flat y-o-y, as automakers ran down inventory. 

According to the Brazilian non-ferrous metals association **Sindicel** , in April, sales of copper for the infrastructure sector (energy, transmission, and conducting special enamelled wires) were down 20% y-o-y, followed by construction, where volumes retreated by 15% y-o-y and telecoms, which were down by 10%.  Sindicel expects that improved construction and telecoms demand will result in better demand from August.  However, the effects of government housing initiatives will not have any impact on copper demand until next year. 

In Q1 2009, **Caraiba Metais** saw production of wirerod down 30.8% y-o-y and 24.7% q-o-q to 22,218t.  Brass mill **Eluma** saw semi-fabricated products volumes down 20% y-o-y and 13.4% q-o-q to 12,584t in Q1 2009. 

###### **6.1.2 Chile** 

Chile’s economy is expected to see GDP contract by 2.2% and industrial production by 6.9% as a result of the global slowdown.  In large p

art, this fall is due to falling commodity prices, including copper. We expect this to translate into a decline in refined copper demand of 10.5% y-o-y. Due to relatively restrained lending, Chile has not seen the housing bubble experienced in some countries, however construction has still fallen sharply in 2009. It is hoped that Chile’s construction sector may bottom out in Q3, although recovery is expected to be slow. Construction is expected to fall by as much as 2.5% this year. New housing sales, which rose by 8% in 2008, could fall by nearer 25% this year. The reduction of the central bank’s lending rate to a record low and a boost in government spending has helped the sector rally. **Madeco** ’s brass mill division reduced its volumes of sales by 22% y-o-y. It saw revenues in Q1 2009 fall by 55.9% to US$22.3M y-o-y due to lower volumes sold and lower copper prices. Madeco sold its cable operations to Nexans on 30th September 2008. ###### 2.1. The market adjustment: the pressure has shifted from mines to smelters and refineries 

###### **2.1.1. Less strain on copper mines** 

Following Q1 2009, when a few mine production cutbacks were announced, Q2 2009 was pretty quiet in this regard.  Some investment budgets for project development were reduced in Q2 2009, although some other projects under development have been resumed.  The outlook for the rest of this year and 2010 has been revised.  The current CRU copper price forecast for Q4 2009 is US$3,800/t, resulting in an average 2009 forecast of US$4,153/t. 

In the CRU April 2009 Copper Quarterly, the copper price was forecast to remain at relatively higher levels through Q2 2009 compared to the Q1 2009 average.  It was set to fall in H2 2009, particularly towards the end of the year.  However, the extent of the decline is now not expected to generate significant cutbacks, as was the case in the April 2009 Copper Quarterly.  The higher copper price forecast also means a positive start to 2010.  Later on, another period of price pressure is forecast beginning in late 2010 deepening into 2011, thus we still anticipate cutbacks coming in 2012 - 2013. 

The strain on copper mine production during the remainder of 2009 and through most of 2010 will be low and no additional major cutbacks are anticipated.  The concentrates market has eased and we expect it to be in balance in the second half of the year (see section 5). 

Over this period, the pressures and cutbacks are expected to shift from mines to smelters and refineries.  The sulphuric acid market is currently in oversupply, which is a problem for smelters as they have difficulty selling the sulphuric acid they generate and especially for those relying on the spot market for sulphuric acid.  Any refineries that are integrated with affected smelter operations are likely to be hit and may need to cut production.  This is the case especially for most refineries in Japan and Korea, whose output altogether represented 15% of the world‟s copper cathodes produced at electro refineries in 2008.  CRU expects cutbacks and/or closures to result a loss of 420,000t of refined copper in 2009.  The most vulnerable smelters are those relying on the spot market for their sulphuric acid disposal (see section 4.2). 

In 2010, only 200,000t of mine cutbacks are anticipated as the copper price is expected to be high for most of the year.  In addition, it is likely that producers may be reluctant to react to short term fluctuations as in the previous downturn (2008 – 2009), as the copper price recovered fairly quickly.  It is likely that companies will prefer to delay or defer project developments rather than close operating mines. 

In 2011, new smelter and refinery capacity will be coming on stream in China.  This is likely to put pressure on the availability of concentrates and some smelters

will again be forced to cut back. This will be exacerbated by cutbacks which are anticipated as the copper price will continue a downward trend that is expected to begin in 2010. By 2012 – 2013, higher copper prices are expected to prompt restarts at idled mines, but we expect that projects will have been delayed by the low prices in 2010 - 2011 (see section 3). The Chilean operations, where most labour contracts will be negotiated by the end of 2009, produced 1.625Mt of copper in 2008 altogether (10% of world copper production in 2008). Earlier this year, labour contract negotiations at Lomas Bayas included an 8-day strike and a 4% pay increase, among other benefits. Local newspapers suggest this strike is a precedent for the forthcoming collective negotiations. In Australia and North America fewer labour contract negotiations are due this year. - Redundancies: no further major redundancies have been announced after the big rounds in Q4 2008 and Q1 2009. In some cases workers have been claiming “unjustified lay-offs”, but still the risk remains low. In the African Copperbelt, it is not clear if the risk of industrial action has reduced compared to previous months. ###### **3.1.3. Technical faults** The rush to run equipment at high utilisation rates has passed, and so has the risk related to technical faults. That risk is now much lower, although unexpected breakdowns can never be ruled out. However, it has, in effect, been replaced by worries over the maintenance and replacement of equipment, as companies cut working capital and investment budgets. It might be the case that maintenance has not been done properly and, in addition, the reduction in working capital has affected mine equipment suppliers, who have had to draw down their stocks. For example, Caterpillar announced that it will reduce its inventory by about US$3B in 2009. CRU believes that, as mentioned in the previous Copper Quarterly (April 2009), in this environment, common technical faults may take even longer to be solved than during the period of high prices. SAG mill and ball mill failures have been announced in Q

2 2009 at Phu Kham (Laos) and Golden Grove (Australia) (see Appendix B). Meanwhile, the SAG mill issues at the Laguna Seca concentrator at Escondida continue and repairs are scheduled for Q3 2009. The SAG mill will be closed for a 45-day period in July and August and it is not expected to return to full capacity before September. On 24th June, Teck announced a geotechnical issue at its Highland Valley mine in British Columbia, the largest copper mine in Canada, which will reduce its forecast production for 2009 and 2010. This is risk that every mine operation faces. It is likely that with the downturn and the implementation of cost saving policies and potential poor maintenance of equipment, we could potentially see more equipment failures in the forthcoming months. ###### **3.1.4. Ore grade decline** In the April 2009 Copper Quarterly, CRU was expecting that, due to the lower commodity prices, some miners would respond by mining higher grade copper ore in order to reduce operating costs. However, data available from Q1 2009 production reports suggest that this was not necessarily the case. Reasons will depend on by-products, the ease or difficulty with which the mine plan can be changed and whether the deposit actually has high grade zones. To address whether mines are high grading we have compared the Q1 2009 copper ore grades against their historical averages, and we presume that if the mine is high grading the copper ore grades may be higher than the historical averages. From a sample of 41 copper mines, of which quarterly ore grade data are available, and which are located in all regions that produce either CRU International Limited confidential Copper Quarterly Report July 2009 Chapter 2 59 copper cathode or copper in concentrates with different by-products, we observe that only 13 (32% of our sample) have higher Q1 2009 copper ore grades than their historical averages. Also, 9 of these 13 mines show an upward change higher than their historical variances when compared to Q1 2008. The other 4 mines have increased their Q1 2009 copper ore grade compared to Q1 2008 within the usual scope of their quarterly adjustments. The mines who are mining lower copper grades are mostly in South and Central America (generally low cost mines and/or facing long term copper ore grade decline) and Europe. The mines where it is possible that they are high grading are in Australasia, North America and Africa. ###### Not clear if copper mines are high grading Q1 2009 copper ore grades vs historical averages

###### **3.1.5. Infrastructure problems** Problems and limitations in infrastructure have continued as in previous months. Zambia experienced blackouts throughout the country, including the Copperbelt, because a major distribution transformer on the national power grid was damaged by fire. The country also imports electricity from its neighbour DR Congo, but this is insufficient to allow mines to run at full capacity. As a result, copper mines reduced their production. It was reported that Equinox Minerals had to suspend operations at Lumwana for 18 hours; and Konkola Copper Mines and Mopani Copper Mines operations were also affected. The Zambian government announced that the country needs US$800M for new power projects and is looking for funding. ###### **3.1.6. Mergers and acquisitions** In Q2 2009, the major M&A activity regarding copper assets reached US$1.5B, down from the US$2.5B of Q1 2009. However, in the following months we expect more companies from Brazil, India and China (together now known as the BIC economies) to be very active in CRU International Limited confidential 60 Copper Quarterly Report July 2009 Chapter 2 purchasing assets. In fact, various Chinese companies have been active in pursuing investment opportunities (mainly in Australia). Xstrata‟s bid for Anglo American may be the major M&A bidding involving western companies. It is likely that all this activity is in response to lower mining equity prices and the emergence of a number of distressed companies and properties. One way or another, mergers and acquisitions can affect production from operating mines and investment decisions for new projects. In particular, it alters the internal decision making of the companies, leading to project reviews and therefore altering the timeline for new projects. Xstrata made a preliminary proposal to Anglo American for a nil-premium merger of the two companies. The Board of Anglo American reviewed the proposal and said that it “lacked strategic merit” and the terms proposed were “totally unacceptable”. Press rumours and analysts suggest that Xstrata may start a hostile bid. If the merger occurs, the company would become the world‟s largest copper mine producer (1,579,000t on a 2008 basis) and third largest copper refiner (1,033,000t on a 2008 basis). Governance issues** Several initiatives in different countries regarding the increased participation of governments in mining companies are being developed. Full nationalisation of mining companies seems very unlikely. Governments, however, are introducing different ways in which to have ownership and influence over mining operations, without actually being involved in operating the mines. The copper price rebound has fostered expectations from governments at producing countries, who are more likely now to exert pressure on projects under development. The government leaders of Zambia, Papua New Guinea, Mongolia and Zimbabwe are reviewing current legislations and contracts in order to have greater stakes in certain copper projects. So far, governments are limiting their stakes to less than 50%. Details have not been published and no certain decisions seem to be taken, although this represents a risk especially given the copper price rebound. In South America, different political issues related to, or involving International Labour Organisation (ILO) Convention No 169, have arisen: - Chile has to fine tune its legislation in accordance with the ILO Convention No 169 by September 2009, and implement it in the following months. This will overlap with the campaign ahead of the December 2009 presidential elections. Some investment decisions may be affected. - In Peru, recent claims from the indigenous population in the Amazonas region successfully persuaded the government to back down from two legislative decrees and this may set a precedent for similar protests across the country, including claims over mining properties. - Ecuador and Bolivia changed their national

constitutions and consequently their mining legislation. ###### **3.1.8. Natural hazards** No major disruptions were reported due to natural hazards. In Chile, the April to July period rainy season was good, although the country still faced a 14% price increase for electricity in June for major companies and some minor energy cuts related to bad weather were reported. In Zambia, Equinox Resources said it will not meet its estimated production for this year (170,000t of copper in concentrates) at its Lumwana mine due to heavy rains and lack of adequate equipment. Late climate reports expect El Niсo to occur in the 2010 southern hemisphere summer (December – March). This may disrupt operations in Peru and Chile. Project development will be pushed back** Production cutbacks are expected in response to the low copper prices expected from late 2010. In 2009 and 2010 an adjustment is anticipated in smelters mainly in response to the sulphuric acid market. However, the situation will change through 2011 to 2013 and pressure will be on new mine projects. In section 2.1 we explained how the market adjustment is set. Here, we explain why new mine projects are anticipated to be affected from 2011 to 2013. The copper price rebound on Q2 2009 has encouraged a reassessment of some projects in order to reduce their capital cost. Development of some projects has even been restarted. We have anticipated that this year, copper mine capital costs could fall by around 20%, easing the development of more capital intensive projects. ###### Potential new capacity deferred and reduced Potential capacity of new copper mine projects 2008-13 (000 tonnes)

There are additional factors that affect the project pipeline and made us delay and push back potential project capacity from 2010, 2011 and 2012 to 2013 and beyond the period of analysis of this Copper Quarterly (see chart below). Firstly, the current fragile financial health of many companies reduces the chances to get funding for new projects. Secondly, the high metals prices over the last few years have enormously increased the expectations of local populations and governments regarding the benefit they can obtain. Local stakeholders in most regions have been empowered and are not willing to accept anything less than in the last few years, especially in the projects where “negotiations” have already started. Thirdly, new projects present challenging geology which may require research and development of new technology. Fourth, governments have more demanding environmental legislations that delay the development stage of a project as co

mpanies need to acquire more permits.  This also applies for other developments that complement the mining facilities, such as power infrastructure or roads.

Fifth, the increasingly financial activity of mining companies may shift their attention from decisions about development those about corporate strategy.  In other words, all the above reasons are extending the actual development period for projects, particularly greenfield projects. 

For the same reasons, we believe that a company will prefer to delay or defer the development of a new copper project rather than shutdown a mine under operation.  To close a mine (and to restart it) some spending is needed for the equipment and labour force.  Local factors (population, government) and the central government may set some conditions or requirements for such closures. 

On a more positive note, smelters‟ and refineries‟ new capacity will be coming on stream, especially in China (see section 4.3).  It can be expected that these facilities will be desperate to purchase copper in concentrates, thus promoting copper concentrate projects to be developed. 

###### **3.2.2. Project development uncertainty** 

We can anticipate more disruptions in 2012 and 2013 as many projects are scheduled to come on stream.  CRU, however, expects that the lower copper price in 2010 and 2011 will discourage development of many of them during the forecast period.  In addition, as said previously, there are increasing challenges for new projects. 

To factor in this uncertainty around higher risk copper mine projects, CRU characterises projects as either “firm”, “probable” or “possible”.  Firm projects have passed feasibility and will go ahead barring any major problems, in fact most of them have started construction or have obtained the correspondent permits and finance.  Probable projects are at the feasibility stage and CRU forecasts that of this only 50% will come on stream in the forecast year. Possible projects are generally still at a pre-feasibility stage and CRU assumes only 25% of these projects will come on stream in the forecast year. 

Projects in 2010 and 2011 are mainly brownfield, expansions and thus aim to optimise the potential of deposits that are already under exploitation.   In 2012 and 2013 most potential new production is greenfield, which means that no mine activity was in place before and it is very likely that the investment will present more difficulties than those mentioned above. 

As we said in the April 2009 Copper Quarterly, most projects due to start-up in 2012 and 2013 are highly uncertain and are still only classed as probable or possible.  Therefore, the copper production that we forecast from new mine capacity is much less than the potential new capacity available.

Overview During the first half of 2009 smelters and refineries continued to suffer from declining markets for their refined copper (with the exception of the Chinese smelters), tight markets for scrap and concentrates, and a global oversupply, with declining prices, of sulphuric acid. Cutbacks and closures were announced in Asia and North America. The good news is that, although refined copper demand is poor in most countries, the copper price has held up. We have not seen the anticipated level of mine cutbacks, with the result that concentrate availability has not fallen as expected. This factor, together with smelter and refinery cutbacks, means that the concentrates market has eased a little, although we are still forecasting a deficit for the balance of this year. Reported and estimated data show that, after increasing by just 0.8% in 2008 total refined copper output actually fell by 0.6% year on year in the first quarter of 2009, the first year on year fall since 2003. This was despite the continued increase in capacity, which grew by 5.6% year on year in the first quarter. Capacity utilisation fell to just 68%, well below typical historical levels of 75-80%. The fall largely reflected the announced cutbacks and closures at smelters and refineries in Asia, together with operating difficulties in Asia and Africa, as well as shortages of scrap materials, particularly in China. Cathode production from SXEW operations was up by over 6.9% year on year in the first quarter, but electrorefined production fell by 2.3%, with the recovery of copper from scrap materials down by nearly 15.0%. Much of this fall was accounted for by China. Smelter production was unchanged from a year ago, but capacity grew by 2.8%, resulting in a fall in the average utilisation rate to 69.5%. First half 2009 output of refined copper is estimated to have declined by 3.2%, and for the year as a whole, despite the 1.5Mt/y forecast increase in production capacity, we are forecasting a 6.0% decline to a little more than 17Mt, the lowest level of annual output since 2005. Capacity utilisation will fall to just 65%. All of the decrease will be accounted for by electrorefined output, which is expected to decline by 8.5%. A 5.0% increase is forecast for SXEW output this year due to new mine start ups and the ramp up of capacity brought on stream in 2008. The decline in electrorefined production will reflect the announced cutbacks

and closures of smelters and refineries in Asia, continued difficulties at some operations and expected additional cutbacks due to the oversupply of acid and/or refined copper. A number of producers, particularly in Asia are still having difficulties placing sulphuric acid, and may be forced to cut back in order to reduce their acid stocks. In addition, although the situation has eased, scrap supply still remains tight in China affecting secondary producers and those using a mix of primary and secondary raw materials. Looking further ahead, we expect to see electrorefined copper production resume its growth path. Investment by the Chinese producers will ensure that smelting and refining capacity continues to grow – we are forecasting an average annual increase in smelting capacity of 3.6%, and in refinery capacity of 2.9%. Demand for refined copper and sulphuric acid should improve as the global economy emerges from recession. However, smelter capacity growth is expected to exceed that of mine output, and smelter and refinery production will be limited by concentrate availability throughout the forecast period. n issues ###### **4.2.1. Cutbacks** For 2009 we are now forecasting a decline in smelter and electrorefined output as cutbacks are expected to more than offset any increases in capacity. Although concentrates remain in tight supply, the issue of concentrates availability is now being eclipsed by those of the excess supply of sulphuric acid and poor copper demand, with rising stocks of both commodities. Most at risk in these two years are those smelters and refineries that are suffering from the greatest downturn in demand for their refined copper demand and/or their sulphuric acid. This is mainly the Japanese and North American smelters. In addition, while still enjoying positive growth in copper demand, the Chinese smelters are facing rising stocks of sulphuric acid. However, the availability of concentrates will once again become a more significant factor, and is expected to limit refined copper output. We expect that the Chinese smelters will be the most vulnerable to the shortfall in concentrate availability. Firstly, they still rely heavily on the spot market, while custom smelters in Japan and Europe are covered with their long term contracts. Secondly, the large amount of new capacity due on stream (see section 4.3) will need to secure raw materials, and with most of the production from existing mines tied up under long term contracts, it will be dependent on new mine production, much of which is still uncertain. ###### **4.2.2. ###### **4.2.3. Scrap availability** The availability of scrap for smelting has declined sharply during 2009 due largely to a fall in the rate of gener

ation. Lower levels of economic activity in Western countries has resulted in a decline in the generation of new scrap, while lower levels of consumer spending have also affected the generation of old scrap from construction and the replacement of white goods and other consumer durables. (New scrap is generated during industrial processes or the production of semi fabricated and final products from copper or copper alloys. Old scrap is generated when a product comes to the end of its useful life and is discarded or scrapped). Lower prices at the CRU International Limited confidential 74 Copper Quarterly Report July 2009 Chapter 2 end of 2008 also meant that supplies of scrap to the market dried up. Merchants were reluctant to release material that had been bought at higher prices, while lower copper prices also reduced the profitability of scrap collection. Higher prices in 2009 have seen some improvement in the availability of scrap to the market, although generation rates remain low. As a result scrap discounts have fallen sharply, making scrap more expensive, while Chinese smelters have not been able to secure sufficient raw materials to be able to operate at planned levels. Traders were reluctant to sell to the Chinese at the end of 2008 after a number of Chinese traders defaulted on contracts, but this has now been resolved, particularly as the Chinese traders have been offering very favourable discounts in order to secure what material they can. It is mainly the Chinese and Russian smelters and refineries that have been affected by the decline in the availability of scrap materials. West European producers are able to procure sufficient materials to produce to plan, but they are being forced to accept lower discounts in order to secure material. A shortage of material has forced a number of Chinese producers to cut back or even close. Two major Chinese secondary producers, Ningbo Jintian and Shandong Jinsheng closed at the end of 2008, and although production has resumed it is at a much reduced level. Other smelters that treat a mix of concentrates and scrap have turned to the concentrates market. Reported figures show that total Chinese production from scrap fell sharply at the end of 2008 and into the first quarter of 2009, but it has recovered in the second quarter. Primary output has been relatively stable. Russian production from scrap has also declined as producers are unable to secure sufficient material. Imports of scrap, which are mainly from Kazkahstan, have fallen sharply over the last six months, while domestic generation has also declined. The concentrates balance The concentrates balance is estimated to have shown a statistical deficit during the first half of the year. However, higher than expected mine output coupled with smelter cutbacks mean that the deficit was smaller than originally forecast. We have not seen the level of mine cutbacks forecast earlier in the year because the copper price has remained high enough for most mines to continue to cover operating costs. Indeed, some African producers have announced that they are reversing previously announced cutbacks/closures. Although the concentrates market is expected to remain in deficit through the second half of the year, this will be smaller than previously forecast and stocks should now be sufficient to cover the shortfall. The 45-day closure of one of the SAG mills at the Escondida mine will result in a substantial loss of output, estimated at 250,000-300,000t, but this was known about well in advance and smelters have taken steps to ensure that they are covered for this loss. Mine supply is expected to fall short of smelter demand throughout the remainder of the forecast. However, expected smelter cutbacks during the remai

nder of 2009 and 2010 in response to poor cathode demand and the oversupply of sulphuric acid will substantially reduce this shortfall, particularly as we do not now expect to see any demand related mine cutbacks until the second half of 2010. The concentrate deficit will increase through 2011-2013 due to the combination of mine cutbacks and delays to projects in response to the lower prices forecast for 2010-2011. Thus there will continue to be downward pressure on TC/RCs. ###### Global deficit in mine supply will grow Actual/forecast mine Output

Recent concentrate market trends Strong demand from the Chinese smelters brought a tighter tone to the spot concentrates market in the first quarter of 2009, and the market continued to tighten through the second quarter. Mine offerings continued to be few and far between, sentiment among traders remained bullish and Chinese demand remained strong. The Shanghai/LME arbitrage was positive throughout most of the quarter until the end of June, favouring importing. Chinese smelter output was up year on year, requiring increased tonnages of concentrates, and imports for the first five months were also higher. The two main Indian smelters also came back into the market to buy, although Sterlite has once more retreated from the market as continued operational problems have again resulted in rising stocks at the smelter. The other Asian and European smelters continued to be covered with their long term contracts. There have been few offerings from miners, whose output is fully committed under their long term contracts. Over the last month, the only tenders have been for 2010 delivery. After rising by 15% in 2008, Chinese concentrate imports for the first five months of the year were up by 6.5% year on year. There have been notable increases from some sources, including new mines in Laos and the Dominican Republic, and also from Iran and Kazakhstan. ###### 5.2. Both Sterlite and Birla Copper also bought at low terms. However, this was the low point. In early June the Shanghai/LME arbitrage moved into negative territory, lifting the breakeven TC/RC for the Chinese smelters. Recent trends ###### Prices up, but showing signs of losing momentum in July Copper prices maintained a steady upward march from Q1 into Q2. The 3-month prices ended April at about $4,500/t, and by the end of May had reached $4,780/t, before swiftly breaking through to $5,381/t on 11th June. Since then prices have largely moved sideways in a wide range. Late June saw a retreat, with 3-month prices falling to a low of $4,690/t as market participants became more cautious about the strength of the economic recovery and that the China buying spree may be ending. Prices ran back up to a high of $5,345/t by 17th July, but this was accompanied by low trading volumes, which indicates that the rally was driven more by lack of sellers rather than increased buying. The global copper market is becoming more and more polarised between China on the one hand and the rest of the world on the other. In Q1 2009, after discounting the SRB build up in copper stocks, the global market was in surplus by 382,000t. However, the strong demand from China (net imports were 1.8Mt in H1 2009 or 20% of world production in the period) meant that the balance swung into a 55,000t deficit in Q2. However, when looked at on a China/Rest of wo

rld basis, the effect of high Chinese imports soaking up the world’s surplus copper meant that from a 275,000t surplus in Q1 the market outside of China shifted into a deficit of 321,000t in Q2. This helps explain why LME and Comex exchange stocks fell by 224,000t in Q2 and LME prices continued to climb, instead of stocks rising sharply and prices falling as anticipated in the April Quarterly. In addition, prices are likely to have been supported by many pension and other large investment funds reallocating a portion of their portfolios to commodities, including copper, in Q2, driven by the fear of missing out on further price rises. ###### Copper price hits $5,000/t LME cash price & moving averages, 2005 – 17 th July 2009

Short term market outlook ###### Worst avoided… The economic uncertainty and its impact on sentiment will dictate developments in the copper market in the next 12-18 months. This will in turn set the scene to understanding developments over the longer term. The global economy no longer faces the prospect of Great Depression 2.0. However, this is not to say that the economic outlook has improved; CRU’s world industrial production forecast is worse than in April, with an expected decline of 8.6% in 2009 vs. 8.3% previously, and global GDP now expected to fall by 2.5% vs. 2.3%, both due to a lower OECD projection. ###### …but demand still down by 10% in 2009 The much anticipated economic recovery will be slow. In addition, the growth of copper demand will vary across the globe, depending on regional and end-use recovery. From a regional perspective, China will lead global economic and copper consumption growth. Favoured by proximity, South Korea and Taiwan are anticipated to experience a relatively fast recovery as well. In fact, both countries have already exhibited m-o-m rises in copper semis production in Q1 and Q2 2009. Copper demand in regions such as the Middle East, the Indian Subcontinent, South America and the ASEAN countries is also expected to recover fairly swiftly, though at a slower pace, powered by heavy infrastructure projects. Substantially slower demand growth is expected in the industrialised countries, especially in the US, the UK and Spain. From an end-use perspective, the growth of copper demand will mainly be driven by heavy electrical infrastructure projects but equipment manufacturing will also play an important role. The weakest demand growth contributor will be the ailing building construction industry. Physical demand is more straightforward to predict, the investment side depends on market sentiment. In Q2, with Chinese prices falling, it is most likely that investment funds in commodities m

arkets supported copper prices far above the equilibrium levels governed by demand and supply dynamics.  Even though physical demand for copper remains weak, prices were inflated by investment activity triggered by early recovery signs.  It remains to be seen whether this positive momentum is sustainable.  CRU believes that prices will come under pressure once the poor fundamentals outlook reasserts itself. 

Despite the early economic recovery signals, copper semis producers in the world excluding China generally report they have limited visibility of consumption prospects, as order volumes remain low with customers operating on a hand-to-mouth basis.  This is especially the case in industrialised countries in the northern hemisphere, which in Q3 sees seasonally slower demand anyway.  In addition, this year’s summer holiday shutdowns will be extended by a week or two to keep inventories under control at many semis plants and their customers.  Overall, demand in the world outside of China has largely been meeting the expectations we had in April, with total consumption on course for an 18% decline in 2009 as a whole. 

However, we have raised our Chinese consumption forecast for 2009, with growth of 10.3% now predicted, which means the decline in global growth is now only 10.1% to 15.9Mt vs.

###### Cutback pressures solely on smelters/refineries 

As copper prices maintained an upward trend from the low of $2,980/t in December 2008 they are now well above the industry cost curve, meaning all mines that remained open are profitable.  As a result, we will not see the further 620,000t of cutbacks in mine production this year that we had outlined in the April Quarterly.  Mine output in 2009 is therefore forecast to be higher than projected three months ago, especially as some re-openings have now been announced. 

Adjustments on the supply side are now expected at the smelting/refining stages.  Not only are smelters struggling to offload their sulphuric acid but global demand for refined cathode is sharply reduced.  The Japanese smelters/refiners, for example, have confirmed that they will extend their 10% production cutback to the end of 2009 for both acid and cathode reasons. Following an analysis of past performance, we have also raised our disruption allowances across the supply pipeline. 

###### Chinese imports to fall in H2 2009 and prices to follow 

As noted in the Recent Trends section, Chinese imports have been a major driving force of higher prices thus far in 2009.  We expect lower imports into China in H2 as demand growth decelerates and with it a weaker copper price

. Without any increased demand outside of China, the global market balance should move into surplus over the July to December period, the majority of which will accumulate outside of China. Much of this surplus should end up on the exchanges, leading to downward pressure on LME prices. In addition, the run up in prices in mid-July was accompanied by low trading volumes, indicating that a lack of sellers, not increased buying, was the driver which should be bearish for prices when sellers return to the market. However, the wave of investment money will provide a support and we now do not expect prices to fall back as far as we had previously anticipated. We now forecast that the LME cash price will fall to average of $3,800/t in Q4, compared to the $2,650/t forecast in the April Quarterly. ###### When will the SRB resume buying copper? Sentiment about China ‘s cathode imports has been a key driver of the copper price over the past six months. SRB (State Reserve Bureau) restocking kicked off the rebound in prices in Q1 this year. One key factor that will determine sentiment over the rest of this year is whether the SRB will continue to build its copper inventories. The NRDC (the National Reform and Development Commission, the parent agency of the SRB) recently made two announcements about official central government re-stocking of copper in China. Firstly, that there had been 290,000t of copper bought by the central government and secondly that their stockpile had increased by 235,000t. We take that to mean that the SRB booked 290,000t and if the rumours of SRB selling are true, sold 55,000t, leaving a net 235,000t increase in the agency’s stockpile. We do not expect that the SRB will come back into the market to book more copper until the price falls towards, if not below, the $3,500/t level at which it started buying in Q4 2008. Our discussions with market participants in China indicate that Chinese copper buyers generally feel that a fair copper price is around the $4,000/t level. The vast quantities of copper imported by China in H1 2009 are well beyond the level needed to meet its demand requirement. We estimate that there has been a build up in off-warrant stocks in China of over 400,000t in H1 2009 (excluding the 235,000t of SRB build). About 100,000t of this can be attributed to

re-stocking of cathode at semis plants after excessive destocking in Q4 2008 and a further 100,000t to the build up in working stocks at new wire rod mills. However, that leaves over 200,000t of off-warrant stocks that we believe have been built up at traders and among speculative players. 

As has been the case for the past two years, we expect to see Chinese domestic production rise sequentially throughout the year, leading to a lower import requirement in H2.  In addition, the build in off-warrant stocks will take time to be unwound, especially given our forecast of a slowdown in consumption growth in H2.  Chinese copper buyers like to actively manage their stock levels in a bid to buy low and sell high.  Therefore, while they may feel $4,000/t is a fair price, they will restrain their copper buying if they anticipate a fall in the price.  Implicit in our price forecast of $3,800/t in Q4 2009 is a fall to the $3,500/t level for a time in the quarter. Therefore, we would expect the SRB to book the remaining 165,000t of the 400,000t requirement announced by the NRDC earlier this year.  Actual delivery is likely to be spread over Q4 2009 and Q1 2010, with the bulk of it arriving in the New Year.

###### 2010 – A tale of two halves 

The recovery in demand outside of China will be driven by restocking in 2010, as underlying demand begins to improve modestly alongside the broader economy.  The current forecast calls for a 6.8% increase and with Chinese demand set to expand by 8.4%, we forecast global demand growth of 7.4% next year.  Refined output will also recover in 2010, after falling by 6.0% in 2009, leaving the market in a 490,000t surplus, excluding a further 105,000 build in SRB stocks. 

2010 will be a tale of two halves.  Restocking led demand will be concentrated in H1 2010, such that the global market will be in a deficit of over 240,000t.  We therefore expect LME prices in the second quarter to recover to average $4,700/t.  We forecast that refined production growth will continue to increase throughout the year, as new mines are ramped up.  As restocking comes to an end and underlying growth is expected to be relatively anaemic, demand growth will slow in H2.  As a result, the global market balance will move into a surplus of over 700,000t.  The modest draw down in stocks in H1 will mean that, according to the fundamentals, a fall in prices is required if this imbalance is to be kept under control, and we expect prices to average $3,500/t in Q4 2010.  Prices this low should prompt cutbacks at high cost mines, and could lead to another wave of mine project delays in a repeat of the Q4 2008/Q1 2009 response.
