Medium term outlook ###### A delicate balance We have not significantly altered our outlook for 2011-2013 from that presented in April. Above trend growth of 5.3% in demand over the period will be driven by economic stimulus spending and continued economic development in emerging markets, both of which are infrastructure heavy. As always, China will lead the way, expanding by an annual average 9.8%. Production growth of 3.6% per year is forecast to be slightly lower than that presented in April, with the change derived from slightly lower committed production over the period and a higher disruption allowance. We feel that the risks to the disruption allowance are now more evenly balanced, given the high number of mine projects ramping up over the period. Firm greenfield projects coming on in 2011-2013 account for 28% of the increase in total committed mine production over the period. Copper miners will continue to face the challenges of infrastructure development and long term grade decline. Mine supply is expected to fall short of smelter demand over the forecast. However, the expected smelter cutbacks during the remainder of 2009 and 2010 will bring the concentrates market broadly back into balance in 2010. We expect the low prices in 2010 to prompt cutbacks at operating mines and

delays to projects, particularly over the second half of the year. The pace of mine cutbacks will begin to ease back in 2011 and should be totally reversed by 2013 as prices rise. On the other hand, the impact of mine project delays on our refined production forecast is expected to build up over the period. Consumption growth will outpace that of production and the market will move back into a modest deficit by 2011. However, prices will be at a low level at the beginning of the year and the inventory built up over 2009 and 2010 will restrain the price increase such that the annual average will be $1.66/lb ($3,650/t) that year. 2011 will be the low point in the price cycle and will result in mine cutbacks and put a brake on project developments. In 2012, though, the draw down in stock levels as refined demand growth outpaces that of refined production mean prices begin to climb again, averaging $2.13/lb in 2012 and rising further to an average of $2.50/lb by 2013. **The signs of incipient recovery are mounting in Asia and other developing economies.** For instance, second quarter growth in China and Singapore exceeded expectations by some way. The pick-up in Asia is mostly in the wake of the acceleration in growth in China’s domestic sector.  And that has its origins in China’s stimulus package, which is starting to translate from investment into output.  To that extent **China’s and Asia’s recoveries look sustainable over an 18-24 month horizon.** The turn-around in Singapore, however, was rooted much more in the inventory cycle, and similarly export-dependent economies are likely to experience rather less dynamic upturns than China because the developed economies lag a quarter or more behind them, and face much greater obstacles to their recoveries. 

**At present there is little to suggest that final demand, principally consumer spending and investment, are anywhere close to mending properly in the developed economies.** In some cases, indeed, final demand is still deteriorating, albeit at a slower pace than before.  The USA should be the first to improve, in the wake of its stimulus programme, but the upturn will be arduous, there and elsewhere in the developed world.  The problem for many of these economies is first that their domestic imbalances are far from unwound yet.  Second, although the worst of the financial crisis appears to be over, many consumers and firms remain locked out of credit markets in developed economies. 

**In summary China has begun to provide a short-term boost to Asia, but is incapable of offsetting the drag from the developed economies on its own.** 



**In the USA indicators suggest that the stock clearout should come to an end this** 

**quarter.** But there is little to indicate that domestic demand has any momentum behind it. That will have to wait until the main part of the fiscal stimulus starts to work, and that will be later rather than sooner. 

**Europe** lags even further behind, and still faces strong headwinds. 



**China’s domestic economy is on the mend.** Indeed, parts may even be recovering too fast. As a result the outlook for China is subject to some upside potential in the short term.  There is a risk now, however, of fresh bubbles forming, so the prospects for 2010 are slightly less assured than they were.

**The hard activity data is starting to bear the forward-looking indicators out.** Industrial production fell by 0.4% month-on-month in June, thanks in part to a deceleration in the rate of contraction in the production of investment goods. But final demand remains weak by past standards, and is unlikely to rally any time soon,** not just because households are busy rebuilding their balance sheets, but because of feedback effects from the cycle itself. Although corporate earnings have started to surprise on the upside again **firms continue to cut their costs and investment.** In the past upside earnings surprises have heralded a turn in the output cycle. A consequent turn in the investment cycle remains a long way off, however. **Industrial capacity utilisation fell to a new record low of 68% in June, and with so much excess capacity around it will be many many months before a pick up in output translates into significant business investment.** More probable is a gradual slow down in the rate at which capital spending is contracting. The emergence of much spare capacity is weighing on labour costs as well: wages are largely stagnant. **So unemployment has further to rise, and household confidence remains wobbly as a result,** although there are signs that the rate at which jobs are being lost is moderating, despite 467,000 losses in June. The University of Michigan’s index of consumer sentiment was discouraging in July, falling from 70.8 in June to 64.6, as a result of that and other adverse influences. **Therefore consumers continue to pay down their debt,** lifting the personal savings rate to almost 7% in May, it’s highest since late 1993. And those that can’t are defaulting on their credit card debt in increasing numbers, as well as on mortgages. Consumer spending continues to suffer accordingly. Thus retail sales excluding cars and gasoline were down by 0.2% monthon-month in June. **On this analysis there is little inherent to the domestic sector in the USA to recharg

e it in the short to medium term; which is where the stimulus comes in.** The tax rebate element of the fiscal stimulus is only a couple of months old.  But at the moment it’s being absorbed by higher gasoline prices and saving. **What it’s doing is preventing an even worse fall in consumer spending then we’ve seen.** On its present targeting it’s unlikely to give activity a decisive lift.  Much therefore hinges on the spending part of the stimulus. 

**The investment element of the fiscal stimulus won’t start to make a difference until the end of 2009 at the earliest.** Government officials estimate that only 25% of the total stimulus will be disbursed this year, 50% in 2010, and most of the balance in 2011.  The original intention was that upwards of 35% of the stimulus would be disbursed in 2009, and almost 60% in 2010.   The investment portion is being spent even more slowly.  Only 3% of the Transportation Department’s allocation of $21.2 billion has so far been spent, for example. 

**This money can’t arrive a moment too soon, however: construction spending fell to its lowest level so far in this downswing in May.** It probably steadied in June, in the wake of a pickup in housing starts, but with inventories of unsold new homes still far above average levels the house building sector is in no shape to provide a boost to activity any time soon. 

**This is why growth in the USA is unlikely to top 3% until 2011.  And even then the recovery will be a little more muted than those of the past.  The drags will remain significant on the one hand, and the stimulus drawn out on the other.**

###### 2.2 Europe: drag from unemployment intensifying 

**Our forecast for economic activity in the Eurozone is little changed this month since recent economic developments in the region have been in line with our expectations.** 

**Industrial production is rebounding but the improvements in the sector have been the result of government support and the easing of the stock cycle rather than strong final demand.** A number of countries in the Eurozone posted an increase in industrial output in May. Particularly encouraging was the 3.7% month-on-month rise in German industrial production. German manufacturers have benefited from the pick

-up in activity in Asia with output of capital goods rising by 8.3% month-on-month in May.  Scrapping schemes enacted by governments across the Eurozone have brought about a strong boost in demand for small cars, propping up the auto industry.  Nevertheless, given the very sharp falls in production over the last two quarters, it will be some time before we see a meaningful recovery in the industrial sector **.  And we expect the recovery to slow again once the build up of inventories has ended because the fundamentals remain weak.** 

**In particular domestic demand will continue to be a significant drag on growth.  Both** 

**the consumer and corporate sectors continue to face difficulties in securing and repaying credit.** And anaemic domestic and international demand will continue to force firms to **cut employment over coming months** in response to falling profits. **Eurozone unemployment reached a 10-year high of 9.5% in May** with a strong impact on retail sales.  Wholesale and retail trade volumes excluding cars registered a 3.3% decline in May and headline inflation turned negative at -0.1% for the first time since the introduction of the euro.  And given that much of the recent strength of purchases of durable goods such as cars has been the result of temporary government incentives bringing forward demand, we expect **overall household consumption to remain weak next year also.** 

**The outlook for corporate investment is equally poor.  Banks remain under stress with strong negative implications for the corporate sector.** Over the last ten years bank loans have  financed over 50% of firms’ capital expenditure in the Eurozone compared to just 35% in the USA.  Due to a combination of depressed demand, as firms cut investment, and tighter bank lending standards, lending growth continues to fall despite the European Central Bank’s efforts to enhance liquidity and ease credit conditions.  In June the ECB remained supportive, keeping its refinancing rate at an all time low of 1% and making a €442 billion one-year loan to banks in the Eurozone. 

**While domestic conditions in the Eurozone remain gloomy, the external sector is not providing much support to the economy either.** The deterioration in exports has slowed over

And with credit availability remaining restricted, consumer spending looks set to be a strong drag on growth at least for the rest of the year. ###### 2.3 Asia: domestic sector warming up in China ###### **Asia’s in the vanguard of the nascent recovery. And China’s at the forefront of that** **vanguard.** The momentum building in China stems from its fiscal stimulus, and the flood of credit that has accompanied it, and is very largely domestic in nature. With one or two exceptions the stimulus packages elsewhere in Asia, although sharing a bias towards investment, are smaller in scale. **Therefore the other export-orientated economies in Asia are benefiting as much from China’s policies, in so far as they ship finished goods and durables to China, as from their own.** India, like China, is more dependent on a pick-up in domestic demand, however. © 2009 CRU International Limited confidential

**China will therefore head the league table of recovering economies, because of the scale and orientation of its policy makers’ intervention,** and it’s already showing signs of recovering more rapidly than we expected **. Indeed, it now looks well on course to achieve its 8% growth target this year. Others will benefit, but be more constrained** by the weakness in final demand elsewhere, because the region as a whole remains heavily dependent on exports to developed economies, and almost two thirds of inter-regional trade in Asia is in components for assembly and ultimately shipment to developed economies. So far, therefore, improvements CRU International Limited confidential Metals Quarterly Report July 2009 Appendix A 115 in a number of Asian economies are as much related to the end of de-stocking, at home and in China, as to improvements in underlying demand. **The Chinese economy shifted up a gear in the second quarter.** GDP growth accelerated from 6.1% year-on-year in the first quarter to 7.9% in the April-June period. **As a result of this faster-than expected upturn we’ve lifted our forecast for GDP growth in 2009 to 8%, and our forecast for growth in industrial production to around 9%.** Our forecasts for 2010 are little changed. But the second quarter data indicates that the stimulus is being disbursed more quickly than we expected, which means that its effects will start to wind down earlier as well, which is why we’ve trimmed our 2011 forecast to a degre

e. 

**That this growth was mostly domestic in nature is born out by the data for investment.** Overall investment in fixed assets in the first half of the year was up by over 33% in nominal terms.  Growth in urban and rural areas was at a very similar pace.  Regionally, however, investment in the western provinces was considerably stronger than elsewhere.  The spending was led by railway projects, which more than doubled on year-ago levels, followed some way behind by road and environmental schemes. 

**The investment spending is beginning to translate into activity in factories.** Whereas industrial output only expanded by around 5% year-on-year in the first quarter, it increased by just over 9% in the second.  Indeed, industrial production appears to be heading back into double digit growth.  In June it expanded by close to 11% year-on-year.  It last grew at those rates in the third quarter of 2008. **Significantly the upturn appears to be spreading to heavy industry:** power output was up for the first time in eight months in June, by 3.6% year-on-year. 

**Imports also signal that the domestic economy is gaining new momentum.** They were well up in June, by 15.6% month-on-month, although they’ve been flattered by the replenishment of stockpiles recently. 

**The acceleration in growth isn’t entirely dependent on investment in infrastructure projects.** The effects of the surge in lending are showing through elsewhere as well, and in particular in two sectors that are more sensitive to credit that others **.  Total vehicle sales rose by 18% in the first six months of 2009,** assisted by incentives on purchases of small cars, fuelefficient vehicles, and vehicle for use in rural areas.  Car sales were up by a hefty 48% year-onyear in June, and vehicle sales overall grew by 36.5%.   Some motor manufacturers are reportedly struggling to keep up. 

**The property market, meanwhile, has recovered very strongly;** so much so that it may be at risk of overheating again.  Floor space under construction was up almost 13% year-on-year in the first six months of 2009.  More seriously property price inflation has accelerated sharply in Beijing and Shanghai, following the introduction of discounts and incentives for buyers and developers at the end of 2008, and in May 2009. 

**Income growth is providing some additional support to consumption,** albeit on a much more moderate scale.   Disposable incomes increased by around 11% in real terms in the first half of the year. 

**The external sector is likely to be the last of China’s engines of growth to recover.** Exports were up by 7.5% month-on-month in June, as the inventory correction came to an end.

But final demand in China’s developed markets is unlikely to show signs of life until the end of 2009 at the very earliest.  In the meantime Chinese exporters are increasingly targeting the emerging markets them

selves, and in particular India, the Middle East and Africa. 

**We expect domestic demand to strengthen further during the second half of 2009, as capital spending translates increasingly into output at manufacturers.** Indeed, the second quarter performance suggests that our forecast may be subject to some **upside risk in the very short term.** But the evidence from the property market suggests that policy measures could end up over-stimulating key sectors, and that raises the prospect of a policy reversal that might dampen the recovery in 2010. **Balancing these risks out has led us to leave our forecasts for 2010 little changed.** Our experience so far this year also suggests that the stimulus funds are being disbursed quite rapidly.  In other words the effect of policy will be concentrated very largely in 2009 and 2010.  As a result we’ve scaled back our forecast for 2011 slightly. 

**Much like the Eurozone, Japan has enjoyed an upturn in its industrial sector in recent months.** In May Japanese industrial production increased by 5.9% month-on-month following an equally strong performance in April.  And although output is now 14% above February’s low, the base effects imply we are still a long way off a significant recovery in output levels. What is more, **we remain cautious regarding the degree of sustainability of the recent bounce.** The inventory to sales ratio remains high and underlying demand both in the domestic markets and abroad continues to be subdued. 

**The outlook for consumer spending in Japan is particularly poor with further wage cuts expected and the unemployment rate already at a six-year high of 5.2%.** We expect conditions in the labour market to deteriorate further given that firms face very low capacity utilisation ratios and falling profitability.  Thus we expect consumer spending to contract by 1.6% in 2009, to be followed by only a mild recovery of 0.8% next year. **And while households continue to struggle, the corporate sector performance will also disappoint** . We expect fixed investment to post a decline of 17.4% in 2009 as firms continue to cut capital expenditure in order to reduce spare capacity. 

Government stimulus initiatives have been somewhat successful, particularly in boosting demand for environmentally friendly vehicles and sales of electronic goods. However, **the implementation of government packages has so far been sluggish and had limited impact against the negative background of the wider economy. We continue to expect Japanese GDP to contract sharply this year by 6%.** 

**In India the July budget included an additional fiscal stimulus worth 0.5-1% of GDP** on top of the stimulus announced earlier in the year which was worth around 0.3% of GDP.  That additional assistance comes on top of significant monetary easing of 4.25% since October 2008. So now there is some up side potential to Indian growth prospects, at least in the short term. Indeed, the domestic economy is starting to show sign

s of renewed vigour already.  Retail sales in India were up over 7% month-on-month in May, and auto sales increased by a solid 15% year-on-year in the first six months.  There is a downside to these policy measures, however. Thus India’s burgeoning budget deficit is likely to become more of a drag into the medium term.  This is one of the structural reasons why we don’t see India emulating China’s phase of very rapid double-digit growth.

**Elsewhere in the region output is recovering now the inventory drawdown has come to an end.** Singapore in particular has rebounded strongly, albeit from a very weak base.  GDP in the second quarter recovered strongly by 20% annualised quarter-on-quarter, which was far above expectations.  This represented a 3.7% year-on-year fall, following a revised 10% decline in the first quarter.  Our forecasts for Singapore are almost certain to be revised up again as a result.  Growth is also gathering momentum in Taiwan and Thailand.   But in these instances the recovery won’t raise growth rates to their potential until 2011 and 2012, because of the anaemic recovery in prospect for the developed economies. 

**South Korea, however, looks like it will escape more lightly.** The government implemented a stimulus worth more than 2% of GDP in 2009, but supplemented it with specific consumer-orientated incentives, such as a cash for clunkers scheme, and a range of green measures. So the total stimulus for 2009-2013 amounts to about 2% per year.  Domestic demand returned to month-on-month growth for the first time in almost a year in May.  Exports have begun to improve month-on-month, up over 17% in June.  And industrial output was up monthon-month in May for the fifth month in a row.  As a result South Korea should experience a much shallower downturn than many other Asian economies in 2009, and a quicker, sharper recovery.

###### Appendix E: Production forecasting methodology and guide to Chapter 2 tables

## Appendix E Production forecasting methodology and guide to Chapter 2 & Appendix C tables 

The basis for our forecasts of mine, smelter and refinery production is the CRU Copper Raw Materials Database (CuRMat), which contains operational data for mines, smelters and refineries.  The data are shown in Appendix C, on an operation by operation basis.  These include historical production and planned production under ideal operating conditions.  All projects, including probable and possible projects are also included in the Appendix C tables, and our detailed table of projects is now also included in Appendix C.  The start up year is based on company projections together with CRU’s view on what is technically feasible in the time period allowed. 

All projects, including new facilities, expansions and possible reopenings are classified as being either committed, probable or possible, depending on the likelihood of them going ahead.  CRU categorises projects as follows: 

**Firm** Projects where permitting has been successfully completed and financing is well underway.  Construction may already have started.  Except for unforeseen disasters, these projects should be operating in the very near future, within a maximum of 2- 4 years.  It should also be noted that, although these projects are in the final stages, they might very well be held up by other unforeseen factors such as political instability or sharp falls in the metal(s) price(s). 

**Probable** Projects where the full or bankable feasibility study has started or is well underway and a successful outcome is expected. 

**Possible** Feasibility studies have started or are about to start, and there are indications that the economics of the project appear sound.  However, it is not a foregone conclusion at this point that the project will or will not advance to further stages.

Copper Quarterly Report July 2009    Appendix D 

To arrive at our forecasts, firstly we consider planned production from committed operations. This includes all existing operations and projects that are definitely going ahead (firm projects), less planned closures.  A disruption allowance is applied to mine production to allow for unforeseen problems, such as strikes, adverse weather conditions, earthquakes, technological problems etc.  This disruption allowance is not specific to a particular set of operations; rather it is applied to the industry as a whole based on CRU experience. The disruption allowance is independent from any market condition; in fact it just reflects the general production performance of the industry.   Secondly, we consider uncommitted projects.  A probability factor is applied to the total production that would be expected from the projects if they are brought on stream.  This is varied according to expected market factors as, for example, high copper prices

and low TC/RCs are more likely to encourage mine projects to be brought on stream than low prices and/or high TC/RCs.  A higher probability is applied to probable projects than possible projects, and, in addition the probability falls further in the future as the development of new projects becomes more uncertain. 

Forecast production from uncommitted projects is then added to the forecast production from existing operations to arrive at our production forecast. 

In addition, we apply a bottom line market adjustment whenever we consider that this is justified by market conditions.  Such an adjustment has been applied in the July 2009 Quarterly Report because we consider that mine cuts will be necessary to balance the refined copper market.  We forecast that prices will fall low enough in late 2010 to encourage such cut backs, which will remain in place until prices recover in 2012.  However we maintain our market adjustment beyond this date, because we also expect that low prices in 2010 and 2011 will result in delays to mine projects that are due to start up in 2012 and 2013. 

The same methodology is applied to smelter and refined output.  In addition, we apply a market adjustment to smelter and refined production to take account of raw material shortages.  This is made after we have considered a reaction to the markets for refined copper and sulphuric acid. As concentrate stocks are now estimated to be critically low, smelter output is lowered to balance the concentrates market.  Refined production then needs to be reduced to balance the blister market. 

The figures presented in the tables in Chapter 2 and Appendix C represent different stages in the forecasting process.  Table 2.1 summarises our forecasts and indicates the process flow from mines to refined copper by each of the process routes.  The following paragraphs explain how the figures in the remaining tables in Chapter 2 are arrived at.  In all tables, the figures for 2008 and all preceding years are actual figures, based on reported numbers.  Those for 2009 onwards are forecasts. 

###### 1.  Mine supply and raw materials for smelting 

**Table 2.2** shows our forecasts of mine production by copper product, and how these are arrived at.  For copper concentrates and EW mines it shows committed production before and after disruption, the market related adjustment, and our forecasts of production from probable and possible projects.   For other concentrates and cement the figures shown are after disruption. No market adjustments are applied to these figures.  These are our final forecast figures.

**Table 2.6** shows our forecasts of smelter output, and shows the calculations to arrive at our final smelter production forecasts, including all adjustments.  We show committed output before and after the disruption allowance, plus the forecast output from probable and possible projects. Like for mines, this is a proportion of potential new output from uncommitted projects.  We then apply additional market adjustments for a reaction to the refined copper and sulphuric acid markets and to balance the concentrates market. 

Committed smelter output is shown in **table 2.8.** This shows the level of output that we believe could be achieved by existing operations and by committed new capacity, under the assumption that sufficient raw materials are available.  The disruption allowance is applied to the bottom line global figure. 

###### 3.  Refined copper production 

Our forecasts of refined copper production and how we arrive at these forecasts are shown in **table 2.7** .  Output is shown by process or raw material.  Primary electro and fire refined output is total output from electro and fire refining that originates from concentrates.   Secondary output is all output from scrap, either via smelting or anode casting.  Electrowon includes conventional EW from oxide concentrates, as well as EW from sulphide concentrates and RLE output also from concentrates. 

The table shows committed output for electro refined, fire refined, conventional EW, EW/RLE from concentrates and NiCuEW. Each output is considered before and after the disruption allowance. The committed output will correspond to that in tables 2.9 and 2.10.  Then the forecast output from probable and possible projects is added.  As for mines and smelters, this is a proportion of potential new output from uncommitted projects.  For electrorefined output we then apply additional market adjustments for a reaction to the refined copper market and to balance the blister market.  An additional market adjustment is also applied to EW output corresponding to the adjustment made to mine production.

###### 4.  The raw materials balance tables 

**Table 2.11** shows the balance in copper in concentrates and other raw materials. 

The first half of the table (sections A and B) shows the potential shortfall in concentrates for smelting. 

**Section A** accounts for the mine supply of raw materials for smelting.  This has already been described above in section 1. 

**Section B** shows smelter demand, i.e. smelter requirements under ideal operating conditions with no restrictions.  However, the standard disruption allowance has been applied to smelter requirements, and also a market adjustment to account for a response to low copper prices, refined copper demand and sulphuric acid demand. 

The first line in section B shows potential smelter output.  This is the sum of the committed, probable and possible figures in table 2.13.  Our assumed loss from cutbacks due to low prices is then subtracted.  Production of EW and RLE refined copper from concentrates is also added, since this is an addition to concentrate demand. 

From this we subtract production from secondary materials, which reduces concentrate requirements.  However, we then need to add back processing losses, i.e. the copper contained in the concentrates that is not recovered. 

This gives total demand for copper contained in concentrates. 

**Section C** is the balance between mine supply and smelter demand.  This currently shows a large shortfall. 

The second half of the table shows our forecast balance after all adjustments. 

**Section D** shows the cutbacks necessary to bring the market back into balance. **Section E** then shows our forecasts of smelter production and concentrate requirements.  Smelter production corresponds with the figure in table 2.6. 

**Table 2.12** shows the blister balance.  This follows the same layout and methodology as table 2.11.  The first part of the table shows the potential balance based on planned refined copper output. 

**Section A** is forecast blister production (from table 2.6). 

**Section B** shows refinery demand for blister, i.e. requirements under ideal operating conditions with no restrictions on output due to shortfalls in raw materials availability.  However, the standard disruption allowance has been applied, and also a market adjustment for low prices. 

The first line shows potential electro and fire refined output.  This is the sum of the committed, probable and possible figures in table 2.15 after the standard disruption but before market adjustments.  Cutbacks due to low prices are subtracted.
